The biomechanics of sprinting involve a precisely coordinated sequence of muscle activations. During the acceleration phase (the first 30 to 60 meters of a 100-meter dash), the athlete's center of mass is positioned anterior to the ground contact point, producing a net horizontal force. Peak ground reaction forces during elite sprinting reach 4 to 5 times body weight, applied over a contact duration of approximately 80 to 90 milliseconds.

Performance analysis in team sports has been transformed by positional tracking systems (typically GPS-based for outdoor sports, with a sampling rate of 10 to 15 Hz, or ultra-wideband for indoor applications at 20 to 100 Hz). These systems generate spatial-temporal datasets that permit quantification of previously subjective metrics: total distance covered, high-speed running volume (typically defined as movement exceeding 19.8 km/h), and acceleration-deceleration loads.

The relationship between training volume and injury risk follows a well-documented pattern. Acute-to-chronic workload ratios (the current week's load divided by the rolling four-week average) between 0.8 and 1.3 are associated with the lowest injury probability. Ratios exceeding 1.5 (i.e., acute spikes) increase soft-tissue injury risk by a factor of 2 to 4, depending on tissue type and training history.
